Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-02
Time: 15:30 PT
Duration: 56 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Liam Chen (Redwood SE), Alicia Romero (Cobalt Head of ML), Greg Dawson (CTO), Samir Patel (Quant Eng)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete):
Quick discovery focused on cost/unit economics and tradeoffs between Hosted, Dedicated, and Private deployments. Customer has high per-day token volume with latency-sensitive inference for trading signals; budget constraints and compliance questions. Redwood AE outlined pricing model, commit discounts for Dedicated, batching/caching levers, and suggested next steps for a small benchmark.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick intro, i'm Maya from Redwood, and with me is Liam who is our solutions engineer. how are you all?
[00:06] Alicia: Good thanks, Alicia here. we run the ML infra at Cobalt, been looking at inference options for a month now.
[00:10] Greg: Greg here, CTO. main question for us is cost predictability and latency.
[00:14] Samir: Samir, quant team. we have bursts around market open, and some requests are short prompts but very sensitive to latency.
[00:20] Maya: Great, that's exactly what we wanted to dig into - the unit economics. quick agenda: get your traffic and cost constraints, go over hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, and then propose next steps including a benchmark. sound good?
[00:30] Alicia: Yup. quick background: we currently run most models on a mix of in-house GPU clusters and an external API for experimental models. rough numbers - 20M tokens/day on average, spikes to 50M during stress, average request size ~120 tokens, mean latency target 150-200ms p95. security is important, SOC2 and some EU data residency concerns.
[00:54] Liam: ok thanks, that's super helpful. couple clarifying q's - when you say 20M tokens/day, is that both input and output tokens or only output?
[01:01] Alicia: both, so total tokens billed includes both directions.
[01:05] Liam: got it. what's your budget target? any per-month spend cap?
[01:09] Greg: currently we have a monthly budget of up to $40k for inference while we validate; long-term we'd like predictability and ideally a model where we can lower unit costs with commits.
[01:19] Maya: perfect. so quick overview of Redwood pricing and levers - Hosted is pay-as-you-go per-token pricing, no infra to manage; Dedicated is reserved capacity with committed monthly / annual discounts which lowers per-token cost and gives predictable throughput; Private is customer-managed private control plane for on-prem or VPC - usually higher fixed cost but needed for strict compliance.
[01:41] Samir: can you give ballpark numbers? rough per-token?
[01:44] Maya: ballpark - for hosted, generative tokens are around $0.XX per 1K tokens for standard model families (note: placeholder, we'll send exact sheet). Dedicated reserved pools can bring unit cost down by 20-60% depending on commit and model quantization. Private has similar unit economics to Dedicated once set up but with additional infra and maintenance fees.
[02:03] Greg: 20-60% is a big range, what drives the gap?
[02:07] Liam: mainly two things - model and quantization profile (fp16 vs int8/nf4), and effective utilization from batching and KV/prefix caching. also whether you use continuous batching to aggregate micro-requests or run latency-optimized single-request paths.
[02:22] Alicia: can you explain caching? like prefix caching? we've tried some in-house caching but it's messy.
[02:28] Liam: sure - if you have repetitive prefixes (like market data + prompt template), Redwood can cache KV cache entries for recent tokens and serve partial generations from cache, which dramatically reduces decoder steps and token compute. we also do prefix dedupe at request layer and suggest moving deterministic scaffold comp to client-side caching. in practice, customers see 10-30% token compute reduction for high-prefix reuse workloads.
[02:52] Samir: interesting. our prompts are 80% templated with different tickers and small variables - seems like a good fit. what about batching - we need p95 < 200ms, batching usually adds latency.
[03:03] Liam: right, batching is a tradeoff. Redwood's continuous batching can do micro-batches with very low overhead and preferential scheduling for latency-critical routes. you can set per-route latency SLOs so critical routes bypass batching or use small batch windows; that affects unit cost. typical trade - if you allow ~50ms extra latency you can batch more and cut token cost by a significant percent; we'll quantify this for your traffic.
[03:25] Greg: what about reserved capacity costs? like how big a commit would we need to get meaningful discounts for our 20M/day?
[03:32] Maya: rough math - 20M tokens/day ~ 600M tokens/month. with hosted at $X per 1K tokens that puts you at roughly $Yk/month (we'll fill exact figures). Dedicated commit tiers usually start becoming attractive around a few hundred million tokens/mo where you can get 20-40% off; larger multi-hundred-million or annual commitments push savings to 50%+. also Dedicated gives predictable throughput which helps during spikes.
[03:57] Alicia: spikes to 50M/day - how fast does Redwood scale? we don't want throttling during open.
[04:04] Liam: Dedicated clusters have autoscale and burst pools; you can purchase burst capacity or configure overflow to Hosted as a fallback. overflow to Hosted can be more expensive but keeps traffic live. for Private, you'd size infra or rely on your infra autoscale which is more manual.
[04:18] Samir: is overflow seamless? concerns about latency jumps and cold-starts.
[04:22] Liam: good point. overflow is designed to be seamless at the request layer; there may be some latency variance when routing to a different region or model variant. we also offer warm pools and priority lanes for the top X% of requests to reduce cold-starts.
[04:35] Greg: curious about quantization and model variants - do you host fp16 and int8 versions? how does that affect latency and quality?
[04:42] Liam: yes, we support multiple quantized builds. int8/nf4 reduces GPU memory and often gives 1.2-2x throughput improvement, slightly different quality in edge cases. Redwood's Optimize recommendations include A/B testing model variants on your prompts to measure quality delta vs cost. that's part of the pilot.
[04:58] Alicia: for compliance we need SOC2, SSO, audit logs, and EU data residency - is that supported on Hosted?
[05:05] Maya: Hosted supports SOC2 and basic region controls; for strict residency or customer-managed keys we recommend Dedicated or Private. Private gives you the most control (VPC + KMS/HSM). we'll attach our compliance pack.
[05:15] Samir: ok - practically i'd like to see a simple cost model: given our 600M/mo tokens, templated prompts, p95 target 200ms, what are costs for Hosted vs Dedicated with a 12-month commit and with and without caching.
[05:28] Maya: agreed - we'll produce a TCO spreadsheet with scenarios: Hosted pay-as-you-go; Dedicated 6/12/24 month commits with burst options; Dedicated + caching + batching; and Private estimate. we'll also include sensitivity to average tokens per request and percent cache hit rate.
[05:41] Greg: sounds good. what about instrumentation? we need token-level cost and latency breakdown per route in our app.
[05:47] Liam: Redwood Console provides per-route token/latency breakdowns, trace hooks, and can export CSV to feed your internal billing. we can add custom tags to track product-level cost.
[05:56] Alicia: any further things we should know for the pilot?
[06:00] Maya: for the pilot we recommend: 1) provide a representative prompt set and 7-day traffic, 2) we'll run a 1M token benchmark across selected model variants and quantizations, 3) test prefix caching with a small replica of traffic, 4) review results and iterate.
[06:15] Samir: timeline? we want results within two weeks.
[06:18] Liam: we can run the benchmark within 48-72 hours of receiving prompts, and send initial cost/perf report in 5 business days.
[06:25] Maya: ok great. we'll do that.
[06:27] Greg: any risks or gotchas?
[06:29] Liam: main things: cache hit-rate assumptions can be optimistic; quantization sometimes alters rare-case outputs - we recommend quality regression checks. Also, for Private there's infra ops overhead.
[06:41] Alicia: cool. let's wrap with next steps.
[06:43] Maya: recap: Maya send pricing/TCO + compliance docs + NDA (due 7/5); Liam run 1M token benchmark (due 7/7); Alicia share prompt set and traffic (due 7/6); schedule deep-dive for private if needed (7/9).
[06:58] Greg: thanks, appreciate it.
[07:00] Maya: thanks all, talk soon.

End of transcript.

References mentioned: Redwood Console (per-route dashboards), TCO spreadsheet (to be shared), compliance pack (SOC2/ISO), example benchmark spreadsheet (link to be shared in follow up).
